# Animal bites

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Emergency medicine > Trauma > Animal bites*

[Original Article Link](/library/ds0oFh)

---

## Summary

<u>Bite wounds</u> can result in physical trauma, bacterial infection, <u>virus</u> transmission, and in some cases, <u>envenomation</u>. The general <u>management of bite wounds</u> involves <u>assessment of the wound</u>, <u>acute wound management</u>, and prophylaxis to prevent infections (e.g., <u>rabies postexposure prophylaxis</u>, <u>tetanus prophylaxis</u>, <u>antibiotic prophylaxis</u>). More specific therapy is based on the location of the wound and the animal that inflicted the wound. Depending on the severity and location of the injury, specialist management may be necessary, e.g., ophthalmology for wounds involving the <u>eye</u> or <u>eyelid</u>.




This article focuses on the bites of nonvenomous animals; see “<u>Envenomation</u>” for more specific information on venomous animals.

---

## Overview

* Common bacterial pathogens:  (from oral flora): <u>Streptococcus</u> spp., <u>Staphylococcus</u> spp., <u>Pasteurella multocida</u>, <u>Haemophilus influenzae</u>, Capnocytophaga canimorsus, <u>Eikenella corrodens</u>, <u>anaerobic bacteria</u> [[1]](/library/MZWMXP0)

* <u>Tetanus prophylaxis</u> indicated for:

* All <u>bite wounds</u> occurring ≥ 5 years after the last tetanus immunization

* All patients with unknown <u>tetanus vaccination</u> status

| <u>Canine bites</u> | <br><br>* Uninfected <u>facial wounds</u> < 24 hours<br><br>* Most other uninfected wounds < 12 hours except hand or foot wounds<br><br><br> | <br>* Depends on <u>patient history</u> and wound<br><br> | <br>* Perform <u>rabies risk assessment</u>.<br><br> | <br>* No<br><br> |

> [!WARNING]
> <u>Primary wound closure</u> is usually inappropriate for hand and foot <u>bite wounds</u> because of the greater risk of infection. [[3]](/library/b2WHTk0)




> [!TIP]
> Human and animal <u>rabies</u> are <u>notifiable diseases</u>.

---

## Management of bite wounds

### Approach




* Begin <u>acute wound management</u>.

* Obtain a focused history on the bite circumstances and <u>immunization</u> history.

* <u>Assess the wound</u>.

* Cleanse bite using <u>wound irrigation</u> and <u>debridement</u> (e.g., with ≥ 1 liter of <u>normal saline</u>).   [[4]](/library/nOW7Gl0)

* Choose wound closure based on the risk of infection.

* Determine the need for <u>antibiotics for bite wounds</u>.

* Determine the need for <u>rabies</u>, <u>tetanus</u>, and additional infection prophylaxis.





> [!TIP]
> Follow local <u>public health</u> protocols as mandatory reporting requirements for animal bites vary regionally.




### Diagnostics




* <u>X-rays</u>

* Indications: suspicion of <u>fracture</u>, <u>joint</u> damage, or <u>retained foreign body</u>

* Findings: <u>fractures</u>, air in the <u>joint</u> space, <u>radiopaque</u> foreign body (e.g., <u>tooth</u> fragment)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* Nonhuman animal bites: not indicated unless the wound is clinically infected

* <u>Human bites</u>: <u>HIV</u>, <u>HBV</u>, and <u>HCV</u> testing of both parties

* Wound cultures: : not indicated unless the wound is clinically infected





### <u>Wound care</u>




* <u>Wound irrigation</u> and <u>debridement</u>: all bites

* Wound closure for bite wounds: Weigh the risk of infection against the need for cosmesis.  [[3]](/library/b2WHTk0)

* Low infection risk: <u>Primary wound closure</u> is likely appropriate.

* High infection risk: Consider <u>secondary wound closure</u> or <u>tertiary wound closure</u>.





| <br>Risk of infection from animal bites [[3]](/library/b2WHTk0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Low | High |
| Nonfacial wound age | < 12 hours | > 12 hours |
| Facial wound age | < 24 hours | > 24 hours |
| Hand or foot involvement | No | Yes |
| <u>Canine</u> or <u>rodent bite</u> | Yes | No |
| Signs of infection | No | Yes |





### Antibiotics for bite wounds




#### Approach [[5]](/library/Om0Ifg)




* Prophylaxis

* Indications

* Wound: moderate to severe wounds, hand or face wounds, penetration of <u>periosteum</u> or <u>joint</u>

* Preexisting conditions: <u>immunocompromise</u>, <u>asplenia</u>, advanced <u>liver</u> disease

* Animal: mammals other than dogs or rodents [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Duration: 3–5 days

* Route: oral <u>antibiotics</u>

* Treatment

* Indications: all infected <u>bite wounds</u>

* Duration: 7–14 days

* Route [[6]](/library/oOW0tl0)

* Mild infection: oral <u>antibiotics</u>

* Moderate or severe infection: IV <u>antibiotics</u>





> [!TIP]
> Obtain both aerobic and anaerobic cultures to guide the treatment of infected <u>bite wounds</u>. [[5]](/library/Om0Ifg)[[6]](/library/oOW0tl0)




#### Preferred agents [[1]](/library/MZWMXP0)[[6]](/library/oOW0tl0)[[7]](/library/hm0c2g)[[8]](/library/LOWwGl0)




* Oral: : <u>amoxicillin/clavulanate</u> DOSAGE [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Om0Ifg)

* IV: <u>ampicillin/sulbactam</u> DOSAGE [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Om0Ifg)





#### Alternative agents [[1]](/library/MZWMXP0)[[6]](/library/oOW0tl0)[[7]](/library/hm0c2g)[[8]](/library/LOWwGl0)




* Oral

* 2<sup>nd</sup> or 3<sup>rd</sup> generation <u>cephalosporin</u> (e.g., <u>cefuroxime</u> DOSAGE) PLUS anaerobic coverage (e.g., <u>clindamycin</u> DOSAGE OR <u>metronidazole</u> DOSAGE), if required [[5]](/library/Om0Ifg)

* <u>Fluoroquinolone</u> (e.g., <u>ciprofloxacin</u> DOSAGE, <u>levofloxacin</u> DOSAGE) PLUS anaerobic coverage (e.g., <u>clindamycin</u> DOSAGE, <u>metronidazole</u> DOSAGE) [[5]](/library/Om0Ifg)

* IV

* <u>3<sup>rd</sup> generation cephalosporin</u> (e.g., <u>ceftriaxone</u> DOSAGE) PLUS anaerobic coverage (<u>clindamycin</u> DOSAGE OR <u>metronidazole</u> DOSAGE) [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Om0Ifg)

* <u>Fluoroquinolone</u> (e.g., <u>ciprofloxacin</u> DOSAGE, <u>levofloxacin</u> DOSAGE) PLUS anaerobic coverage (<u>clindamycin</u> DOSAGE, <u>metronidazole</u> DOSAGE) [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Om0Ifg)

* <u>Carbapenem</u> (e.g., <u>ertapenem</u> DOSAGE) [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Om0Ifg)





### Additional prophylaxis [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* All bites: ensure current <u>tetanus prophylaxis</u>

* Domestic carnivores or known wild reservoirs for <u>rabies</u>: <u>rabies risk assessment</u> and possible <u>rabies PEP</u>

* <u>Human bites</u>: <u>HIV PEP</u> and/or <u>hepatitis B PEP</u>

* Monkey bites: <u>B virus PEP</u>





> [!TIP]
> Foxes, skunks, raccoons, and bats are the main reservoir species for <u>rabies</u> in the US, but all mammals are susceptible. [[9]](/library/KOWUtl0)




### Disposition




* Consult a specialist for complicated wounds. 

* <u>Facial wounds</u> or need for multilayer closure: plastic <u>surgery</u>

* <u>Eye</u> or <u>eyelid</u>: ophthalmology

* Hand infections or <u>open fractures</u>: orthopedics

* Deep tissue infections: general <u>surgery</u>

* Established infections: infectious disease

* Consider hospital admission for:

* Injuries requiring <u>surgery</u> and/or <u>general anesthesia</u> for <u>wound care</u>

* Injuries or infections of deep structures (e.g., <u>tendons</u>, <u>joints</u>, bones)

* Severe infections: <u>cellulitis</u>, <u>lymphangitis</u>, or <u>lymphadenitis</u>

* Wounds at high risk for infection or failed outpatient <u>antibiotic therapy</u>





### Complications of bite wounds [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Structural

* <u>Fracture</u>

* <u>Tendon</u> injury

* <u>Muscle injury</u>

* <u>Joint</u> injury

* <u>Neurovascular injury</u>

* Infectious

* <u>Cellulitis</u>

* <u>Abscess</u>

* <u>Tenosynovitis</u>

* <u>Septic arthritis</u>

* <u>Osteomyelitis</u>

* <u>Sepsis</u>

## Human bites

### Transmissible bacteria




* High risk of polymicrobial infection from oral flora.

* Organisms include <u>Staphylococcus</u> spp., <u>Streptococcus</u> spp., <u>Corynebacterium</u> spp., <u>Fusobacterium</u> spp., and <u>Eikenella corrodens</u>. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)





### Clinical features [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




<u>Signs of wound infection</u> are common as there is often a delay before patients seek health care for <u>human bites</u>.




* Clenched-fist injuries (<u>fight bite</u>): dorsum of the hand is injured when it strikes an individual's <u>teeth</u>

* Small <u>lacerations</u> over the dorsum of 2<sup>nd</sup>–5<sup>th</sup><u>MCPs</u>

* > 50% associated with bone injury

* Up to 20% associated with <u>tendon</u> injury

* Occlusive bites: semicircular pattern of <u>bruising</u>, <u>abrasions</u>, and/or <u>lacerations</u>  

* Commonly located on upper extremity or <u>breast</u>

* May indicate <u>sexual violence</u>, <u>intimate partner violence</u>, or <u>child maltreatment</u>

* Intraoral and oral cutaneous injuries: injuries from the patient's own <u>teeth</u> ranging from small buccal <u>mucosa</u> injuries to through-and-through injuries





> [!TIP]
> Maintain a high degree of suspicion for a <u>clenched-fist injury</u> in <u>dorsal</u> hand <u>lacerations</u> as patients may not initially disclose involvement in an altercation. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




### Management [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[10]](/library/zWWrL40)[[11]](/library/0eWex40)




* Follow the general <u>management of bite wounds</u>.

* Consider <u>primary wound closure</u> for uninfected <u>facial wounds</u> < 24 hours old.

* Consider <u>secondary wound closure</u> or <u>tertiary wound closure</u> in all other cases.

* Provide <u>antibiotic prophylaxis for bite wounds</u>.

* Admit patients with infected <u>human bite</u> wounds and initiate IV <u>antibiotics for bite wounds</u>.  [[11]](/library/0eWex40)

* Test both parties for <u>HIV</u>, <u>HBV</u>, and <u>HCV</u>.

* Provide <u>HIV PEP</u> and <u>hepatitis B PEP</u> to both parties as indicated.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Human bites</u> carry a high risk of polymicrobial infection by organisms such as <u>Staphylococcus</u> spp., <u>Streptococcus</u> spp., <u>Corynebacterium</u> spp., <u>Fusobacterium</u> spp., and <u>Eikenella corrodens</u>. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




> [!WARNING]
> Consider screening for <u>sexual violence</u>, <u>intimate partner violence</u>, or <u>child maltreatment</u> in at-risk patients with human occlusive <u>bite wounds</u>. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




### Complications




* General <u>complications of bite wounds</u>

* Transmission of human-specific viral pathogens: e.g., <u>HIV</u>, <u>HBV</u>, <u>HCV</u>, <u>HSV</u> [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

---

## Canine bites

<u>Canines</u> include domestic dogs, foxes, coyotes, and wolves.




* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[12]](/library/f2WkSk0)

* 85–90% of animal bites

* Children > adults

* Transmissible bacteria [[13]](/library/jNW_aN0)

* Include aerobic and anaerobic organisms that cause polymicrobial infections

* E.g., <u>Streptococcus</u> spp., <u>Staphylococcus</u> spp., <u>Pasteurella multocida</u>, <u>Neisseria</u> spp., Fusobaterium spp., <u>Haemophilus influenzae</u>, Capnocytophaga canimorsus

* Clinical features  ;  [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Location

* Children: often on the head and neck

* Adults: most commonly on the extremities

* Injury pattern

* Varies depending on the size and breed of the dog

* May include <u>contusions</u>, <u>abrasions</u>, <u>lacerations</u>, <u>puncture wounds</u>, and/or <u>crush injuries</u>

* May show <u>signs of wound infection</u>

* Management [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[10]](/library/zWWrL40)

* Follow <u>management of bite wounds</u>.

* Consider <u>primary wound closure</u> for uninfected wounds not involving the hand or foot.

* All other wounds: Consider <u>secondary wound closure</u> or <u>tertiary wound closure</u>.

* Consider <u>rabies PEP</u> for all bites by:

* Wild <u>canines</u>

* Symptomatic dogs

* Asymptomatic dogs that cannot be observed for a 10 day period

* Complications: See “<u>Complications of bite wounds</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> Although <u>dog bites</u> are the leading cause of <u>rabies</u> transmission worldwide, the risk of contracting <u>rabies</u> from domestic dogs in the US is low. [[14]](/library/deWoB40)

## Cat bites

* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[12]](/library/f2WkSk0)

* 5–10% of animal bites

* <u>Cat bites</u> have an infection rate of > 50% [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Transmissible bacteria: similar to <u>dog bites</u>; most commonly <u>Pasteurella multocida</u> [[13]](/library/jNW_aN0)

* Clinical features [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[10]](/library/zWWrL40)[[15]](/library/E6c85W0)

* Location: most common on the hand or fingers

* Often a single <u>puncture wound</u>

* May show <u>signs of wound infection</u> early

* Management [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[10]](/library/zWWrL40)

* Follow the general <u>management of bite wounds</u>.

* Most wounds: <u>secondary wound closure</u>

* <u>Primary wound closure</u> is typically only considered for uninfected <u>facial wounds</u> < 24 hours old.

* Provide <u>antibiotic prophylaxis for bite wounds</u> for all <u>cat bites</u>.

* Consider <u>rabies PEP</u> for all bites by:

* Wild cats

* Symptomatic cats

* Asymptomatic cats that cannot be observed for a 10 day period

* Complications: See “<u>Complications of bite wounds</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> Provide <u>antibiotic prophylaxis for bite wounds</u> (e.g., <u>amoxicillin/clavulanate</u>) with coverage for cat-specific flora (e.g., <u>Pasteurella multocida</u>) because of the high infection rate of <u>cat bites</u>.

---

## Rodent bites

Rodents include mice, rats, hamsters, guinea pigs, squirrels, and beavers.




* <u>Epidemiology</u> [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[15]](/library/E6c85W0)

* Most commonly seen in laboratory workers who handle rodents for research and individuals living in conditions susceptible to rat and mouse <u>infestation</u> (e.g., derelict housing, farms)

* Children > adults

* Transmissible diseases

* <u>Leptospirosis</u>

* <u>Lassa fever</u>

* <u>Tularemia</u>

* <u>Hantavirus infection</u>

* Rat-bite fever [[16]](/library/5VWiE40)

* Transmitted by Streptobacillus moniliformis

* Characterized by <u>fever</u>, <u>rigors</u>, and <u>polyarthralgia</u>

* Can cause severe organ damage (e.g., <u>hepatosplenomegaly</u>, <u>interstitial pneumonia</u>, <u>endocarditis</u>)

* Treatment: <u>penicillin G</u>

* Clinical features

* Commonly located on the face and/or upper extremities

* <u>Bite wounds</u> are usually small

* <u>Signs of wound infection</u> (uncommon)

* Management [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[10]](/library/zWWrL40)

* Follow the general <u>management of bite wounds</u>.

* <u>Rabies PEP</u> and <u>antibiotic prophylaxis for bite wounds</u> are not routinely required [[17]](/library/mVWVE40)

* Complications

* General <u>complications of bite wounds</u>

* Transmission of rodent-specific diseases





> [!TIP]
> Rodents are rarely found to have <u>rabies</u> and have not been known to transmit <u>rabies</u> to humans. [[17]](/library/mVWVE40)

---

## Bat bites

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: Bats can be found worldwide and are typically encountered in caves and rocky crevices, mines, trees, and occasionally in urban and indoor spaces.

* Transmissible diseases: <u>Bat bites</u> cause ∼ 80% of <u>rabies</u> cases in the US. [[14]](/library/deWoB40)

* Clinical features: typically small, painless bites that are difficult to identify

* Management [[14]](/library/deWoB40)

* Follow the general <u>management of bite wounds</u>.

* Use an <u>antiviral agent</u>, e.g., <u>chlorhexidine</u> or <u>povidone-iodine</u>, when performing <u>wound irrigation</u> and <u>debridement</u>. [[18]](/library/0OWeIl0)

* Administer <u>rabies PEP</u> for all the following: [[19]](/library/M2WMRk0)

* Any <u>bat bite</u> or scratch

* Any direct contact with a bat

* Unattended child in the same room as a bat

* Adults in the same room as a bat who may not be able to recall a bite, e.g., intoxicated, deeply sleeping, or have an <u>intellectual disability</u>





> [!TIP]
> Any direct contact with a bat (e.g., touch, bite, or scratch) may transmit <u>rabies</u>. [[14]](/library/deWoB40)
